title: IB Spanish B Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
summary: IB Spanish B common mistakes can cost easy marks. Learn how to read commands, use precise evidence, manage timing, and improve exam performance.
body_markdown:
Imagine a Spanish B student called Elena. She knows the vocabulary, understands the reading texts and can write with reasonable accuracy. Yet when she receives a marked practice exam, the result is lower than expected.


The lost marks did not come from obscure grammar. Elena answered the wrong part of one writing prompt, omitted a unit from a listening answer, copied weak evidence from a reading text and spent so long perfecting her introduction that her final paragraph was rushed.


Elena is hypothetical, but the pattern is familiar. Many **IB Spanish B common mistakes** are failures of exam execution rather than failures of Spanish. The good news is that execution can be trained.


### The quick mistake-prevention checklist


Before submitting an IB Spanish B response, ask:


- Have I followed every command term?
- Have I addressed the required audience, purpose and context?
- Is my chosen text type appropriate?
- Does each comprehension answer include the requested detail?
- Have I preserved necessary numbers, units and distinctions?
- Is my answer supported by the text or audio rather than assumption?
- Have I left enough time to complete and check every section?


For a broader view of the assessment, start with this[IB Language B exam format and strategy guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-to-expect-in-your-ib-language-b-exams-format-timing-and-exam-strategy) .


### Misreading command terms


Elena’s writing prompt asked her to describe a community problem, explain its effects and propose possible action. She produced an elegant description of the problem. Unfortunately, description was only one part of the task.


This is one of the most expensive errors because polished Spanish cannot fully compensate for an incomplete response. Words such as *describe* , *explain* , *compare* , *justify* and *evaluate* require different intellectual moves.


- **Describe:** give relevant characteristics or details.
- **Explain:** show how or why something happens.
- **Compare:** address meaningful similarities, and sometimes differences where relevant.
- **Justify:** support a choice or position with reasons.
- **Evaluate:** weigh strengths, limitations or competing considerations before reaching a judgement.


Do not begin writing as soon as you recognise the topic. Underline the task verbs, circle the audience and identify every required content point. Then turn those requirements into a miniature plan.


For example:


1. Introduce the problem for the intended audience.
2. Explain two effects.
3. Propose two realistic actions.
4. End with an appropriate call to action.


This takes less time than repairing a response that drifted away from the prompt. The[complete guide to scoring highly in IB Spanish B](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-get-a-7-in-ib-spanish-b) provides further guidance on matching writing choices to assessment expectations.


### Choosing the wrong text type or register


A student may understand what to say but package it incorrectly. A formal proposal written like a text message, or a personal blog entry that sounds like an academic report, weakens the relationship between purpose, audience and format.


Before choosing a task, ask three questions:


- Who is speaking?
- Who will read this?
- What should the reader think, feel or do afterward?


Your answer determines the register. A message to a friend can sound personal and direct. A letter to a local authority normally needs a respectful opening, clear organisation and a purposeful conclusion. Text-type conventions should support communication, not become decorative features added from memory.


Build a one-page convention sheet for the formats you study. RevisionDojo’s[Spanish B topics guide for SL and HL](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-spanish-b-topics-your-complete-guide-for-sl-and-hl) can help you connect those formats with course themes and useful language.


### Giving answers without precise evidence


In reading and listening, Elena often understood the general idea. Her problem was precision. When asked why a speaker changed plans, she wrote a plausible reason based on the overall situation rather than the reason actually stated.


Comprehension marks depend on what the source communicates. Your personal interpretation matters only when the question invites it, and even then it must remain anchored in evidence.


Use a simple process:


- Identify exactly what the question requests.
- Locate the relevant line, phrase or moment in the audio.
- Check whether your answer preserves the original meaning.
- Remove information that is merely plausible.


With reading tasks, watch pronouns, negatives, contrast words and time references. *Sin embargo* , *aunque* , *ya no* and *antes* can reverse or qualify the idea you first noticed. With listening, record relationships rather than isolated vocabulary: who did what, why, when and with what result.


The[IB language listening exam structure guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-ib-language-listening-exams-are-structured) explains how prediction and signposting can make audio easier to follow.


### Omitting units, labels or required details


Suppose an audio text says that a journey lasted *tres horas* , but the answer contains only *tres* . The number may be recognised, yet the answer is incomplete or ambiguous if the question requires a duration.


Units are not relevant to every question, and students should follow the wording and mark allocation rather than mechanically copying everything. However, when a number needs a category, preserve it: hours, kilometres, euros, years, percentages or people.


The same principle applies beyond numerical units. If the question asks for two reasons, provide two distinct reasons. If it asks which person expressed an opinion, name the person. If it requests evidence, supply the relevant textual detail rather than a broad summary.


A useful final check is to compare the grammar of the question with the grammar of your answer. If the question asks *¿cuándo?* , your response needs a time. If it asks *¿por qué?* , it needs a reason. This small habit catches surprisingly costly omissions.


### Losing marks through poor timing


A student writes an overlong introduction while the unanswered question and exam clock wait nearby


Elena’s longest paragraph was also her least valuable: the introduction. She kept polishing it because beginnings feel controllable. Meanwhile, the clock continued moving.


Timing problems usually appear in one of three forms:


- spending too long choosing a writing task;
- getting trapped by one difficult comprehension item;
- leaving no checking time for avoidable language errors.


Set checkpoints before the exam. For a writing task, reserve distinct periods for choosing and planning, drafting, and checking. Adapt the exact minutes to your level, approved exam format and personal writing speed. The important point is to rehearse the allocation until it becomes familiar.


During comprehension work, move on when a question begins consuming disproportionate time. Mark it, answer everything else and return later. One uncertain mark should not prevent you from attempting several accessible ones.


Timed work should feel slightly uncomfortable. That discomfort is useful information. It shows whether your strategy survives under pressure, which is why RevisionDojo’s[language acquisition mock exam preparation guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-language-acquisition-mock-exam-prep-november) emphasises exam-like practice rather than unlimited drafting.


### Treating correction as the end of practice


Students often mark a task, read the correct answers and move on. Recognition creates a comforting illusion: once the solution is visible, it seems obvious. But seeing a correction is different from being able to produce the right response independently.


Keep an error log with four columns: task, mistake, reason and future rule. A useful entry might read: “Listening question, omitted *kilómetros* , wrote only the number, always check whether a number needs a unit.”


Then redo the question without looking at the correction. For writing, revise the weak section or rewrite the response after several days. RevisionDojo’s[Spanish B self-study resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-ib-spanish-b-resources-self-study) suggest a balanced routine combining vocabulary retrieval, authentic listening and IB-style practice.


### A better way to practise IB Spanish B


Good preparation alternates between focused skill-building and realistic performance.


Use RevisionDojo’s Questionbank to isolate recurring weaknesses such as command terms, inference questions, text conventions or listening details. Study Notes and Flashcards can then repair the vocabulary or grammar underneath those errors, while AI Chat can explain why an answer missed the demand of a question. Grading tools help turn writing feedback into specific revision targets.


Next, sit timed Predicted Papers or Mock Exams in Exam mode. This tests whether your knowledge remains accessible when the clock is running. The Coursework Library and Tutors can provide additional models and human guidance when a persistent weakness needs closer attention.


RevisionDojo works best as a cycle: attempt, diagnose, repair and retest. Its Questionbank, feedback tools and exam simulation make it the ultimate IB resource for turning small mistakes into deliberate habits.


Elena did not need to become fluent overnight. She needed to stop giving marks away. Read the command precisely, answer with evidence, include the detail requested and respect the clock. Then practise those decisions in the Questionbank and sit timed papers in Exam mode until the better process feels ordinary.
